Re-implementing APGCC: steadying point-based crowd counting with auxiliary points

A walkthrough of the ECCV 2024 paper and my PyTorch re-implementation, built from the paper’s equations.

Paper: I-Hsiang Chen, Wei-Ting Chen, Yu-Wei Liu, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Sy-Yen Kuo, “Improving Point-based Crowd Counting and Localization Based on Auxiliary Point Guidance”, ECCV 2024. Official code: github.com/AaronCIH/APGCC (MIT). All figures and result tables on this page come from the paper and repository. Code repo: github.com/Optimus-Q/APGCC · Written: February 2025

1. The problem: proposals that keep switching

Crowd counting asks two questions: how many people are in the image, and where each head is. Density-map methods answer the first well but need fragile post-processing (“find the maxima”) to answer the second. Point-based methods such as P2PNet predict head coordinates directly and are trained end-to-end, which makes them simple and accurate.

The catch is in training. Every step, a Hungarian matcher pairs each ground-truth head with one of thousands of predicted proposals. Early on the predictions are noisy, so the matcher keeps changing its mind: the proposal that “owns” a head this epoch is often a different one next epoch. Each proposal gets a moving target, and the network ends up under- or over-counting in dense patches.

The authors measure this with an Instability Rate (IR): the share of ground-truth points matched to a different proposal than in the previous epoch. With the plain matcher, IR stays around 0.6–0.8 for all 300 epochs on ShanghaiTech A. APGCC drops it to roughly 0.35 within the first 50 epochs.

2. The point-based baseline (P2PNet)

APGCC keeps the P2PNet framework and adds to it, so it helps to see the baseline first. It has three parts.

Point proposals

The backbone produces a feature map at stride s = 8. Each cell owns K = 4 fixed reference points on a 2×2 sub-grid. For every reference point, a regression head predicts an offset and a classification head predicts a confidence. A proposal is the reference point moved by the scaled offset:

p̂j = Rk + γ·Δj,    γ = 100

REFERENCE POINTS AND PROPOSALS

def reference_points(h, w, stride, row, line, device):
    # (h*w*K, 2) pixel (x, y) reference points for an h×w feature grid
    cx = (torch.arange(w, device=device) + 0.5) * stride
    cy = (torch.arange(h, device=device) + 0.5) * stride
    yy, xx = torch.meshgrid(cy, cx, indexing='ij')
    centres = torch.stack([xx, yy], -1).view(-1, 1, 2)          # one per cell
    return (centres + anchor_shifts(stride, row, line, device)[None]).view(-1, 2)

# in the decoder: proposal = reference point + γ · predicted offset
offset = off.reshape(B, -1, 2) * c.gamma                         # γΔ, γ = 100
out = {'pred_logits': cls.reshape(B, -1, 2),
       'pred_points': refs[None] + offset,                       # p̂ = R + γΔ
       'offset': offset}

Proposal–target matching

Each ground-truth point is matched to exactly one proposal by the Hungarian algorithm. The cost rewards proposals that are close and confident:

𝒟(𝒫, 𝒫̂) = ( τ‖pi − p̂j‖2 − ĉj )i∈N, j∈M,    τ = 0.05 Eq. 1

HUNGARIAN MATCHER

class HungarianMatcher(nn.Module):
    @torch.no_grad()
    def forward(self, outputs, targets):
        bs, nq = outputs['pred_logits'].shape[:2]
        prob = outputs['pred_logits'].flatten(0, 1).softmax(-1)[:, 1:2]   # ĉ_j
        pts  = outputs['pred_points'].flatten(0, 1)                       # p̂_j
        tgt  = torch.cat([t['point'] for t in targets])                   # p_i
        # Eq. (1):  D = τ‖p_i − p̂_j‖₂ − ĉ_j     (τ = 0.05)
        C = self.cost_point * torch.cdist(pts, tgt) - self.cost_class * prob
        C = C.view(bs, nq, -1).cpu()
        sizes = [len(t['point']) for t in targets]
        return [linear_sum_assignment(c[i])                               # one-to-one per image
                for i, c in enumerate(C.split(sizes, -1))]

Matched proposals are positives and everything else is background. Nothing tells the network which proposal should win, and that is the gap APGCC fills.

3. Auxiliary Point Guidance (APG)

The idea is to give the network extra, unambiguous training examples around every head, so it learns what a good proposal looks like before the matcher has to choose one.

  • Auxiliary positives are scattered within ±npos = 2 px of the ground truth. Each should predict high confidence, and its offset should point back to the head.
  • Auxiliary negatives are placed 2–8 px away (±[npos, nneg] on each axis). Each should predict low confidence and a near-zero offset, so it can't “reach over” and steal the head.

Two of each are drawn per head every iteration (kpos = kneg = 2). Because they're resampled every time, the network learns a smooth field: near a head means “confident, point inward”; a few pixels further means “stay quiet”. The proposal nearest the head then wins the match consistently, which is exactly what the IR curve shows.

SAMPLING THE AUXILIARY OFFSETS

def sample_aux_offsets(n, k, lo, hi, negative, device):
    # positives: R ~ U(-n_pos, n_pos)          (n_pos = 2 px)
    if not negative:
        return (torch.rand(k, n, 2, device=device) * 2 - 1) * lo
    # negatives: |R| ~ U(n_pos, n_neg), random sign   (n_neg = 8 px)
    mag  = lo + torch.rand(k, n, 2, device=device) * (hi - lo)
    sign = torch.randint(0, 2, (k, n, 2), device=device).float() * 2 - 1
    return mag * sign

Turning an off-grid point into a proposal

I implemented this step directly from §4.1 of the paper. The prediction heads emit K proposals per query, one per reference slot. For an auxiliary point a, I pick the slot k whose quarter of the cell contains a, then query the features at a − shiftk. That places slot k’s reference point exactly on a, so its prediction is a + γΔ*. This is the quantity Eq. 5 pulls towards the head and Eq. 6 pushes towards zero offset. The auxiliary points go through the same IFI and shared heads as the real proposals, as Fig. 4 of the paper shows.

APG FORWARD (CORE STEPS)

# For every auxiliary point a = gt + R ...
a = (gt[None] + R).reshape(-1, 2)
# 1. which of the K reference slots contains a?
col = ((a[:, 0] % stride) / (stride / line)).floor().long()
row = ((a[:, 1] % stride) / (stride / row_n)).floor().long()
k   = row * line + col
# 2. query IFI at a − shift_k, so slot k's reference point lands exactly on a
q = a - shifts[k]
q_norm = torch.stack([2 * q[:, 1] / Hs - 1, 2 * q[:, 0] / Ws - 1], -1)
ctx = decoder.context([m[b:b+1] for m in maps], q_norm[None], grid_hw)

# 3. same shared heads as the real proposals; keep slot k's output
off, cls = decoder.ifi.predict(torch.cat(per_img_ctx, -1))
offset = off[0][idx, k] * gamma          # γΔ*
logits = cls[0][idx, k]                  # ĉ*
pred   = a + offset                      # p̂* = a + γΔ*

4. Implicit Feature Interpolation (IFI)

Auxiliary points land anywhere, not on grid cells, so the network needs a feature at an arbitrary position. The paper borrows the idea of an implicit function (as in LIIF):

  1. find the 4 nearest latent vectors Z*i around the query;
  2. compute each one’s relative offset δ*i and lift it with a positional encoding φ (sines and cosines at several frequencies) so the MLP can see fine detail;
  3. blend them with bilinear-style weights, where each neighbour is weighted by the area Si of the rectangle between the query and the diagonally opposite neighbour.
Fproposal(x, y) = Σi=1..4 (Si / S) · fθ( Z*i, δ*i, φ(δ*i) ) Eq. 8

IMPLICIT FEATURE INTERPOLATION

def implicit_sample(feat, coords, pe, mode='paper', target_hw=None, eps=1e-6):
    B, C, hh, ww = feat.shape
    centres = grid_query_coords(hh, ww, feat.device).view(hh, ww, 2).permute(2, 0, 1)
    centres = centres.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1, -1, -1)
    ry, rx = 1.0 / hh, 1.0 / ww               # ½ feature cell → the 4 nearest neighbours

    rels, qfeats, areas = [], [], []
    for vy in (-1, 1):
        for vx in (-1, 1):
            c = coords.clone()
            c[..., 0] += vy * ry + eps
            c[..., 1] += vx * rx + eps
            grid = c.clamp(-1 + 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6).flip(-1).unsqueeze(1)
            Z  = F.grid_sample(feat, grid, mode='nearest', align_corners=False)[:, :, 0].permute(0, 2, 1)
            zc = F.grid_sample(centres, grid, mode='nearest', align_corners=False)[:, :, 0].permute(0, 2, 1)
            d  = coords - zc                                        # δ*_i
            d  = torch.stack([d[..., 0] * hh, d[..., 1] * ww], -1)  # in cell units
            rels.append(d); qfeats.append(Z)
            areas.append((d[..., 0] * d[..., 1]).abs() + 1e-9)

    S = torch.stack(areas).sum(0)
    areas = areas[::-1]                       # weight each neighbour by the DIAGONAL area
    # Eq. (8):  Σ_i (S_i / S) · [φ(δ*_i), Z*_i]
    return sum(torch.cat([pe(d), Z], -1) * (s / S).unsqueeze(-1)
               for d, Z, s in zip(rels, qfeats, areas))

POSITIONAL ENCODING φ

class SpatialEncoding(nn.Module):
    # φ(δ) = [δ, sin(δMᵀ), cos(δMᵀ)] with learnable frequencies M (init 2^0 … 2^6)
    def __init__(self, in_dim=2, out_dim=32, sigma=6, learnable=True):
        super().__init__()
        n = out_dim // 2 // in_dim
        m = 2 ** np.linspace(0, sigma, n)
        m = np.stack([m] + [np.zeros_like(m)] * (in_dim - 1), axis=-1)
        m = np.concatenate([np.roll(m, i, axis=-1) for i in range(in_dim)], axis=0)
        self.emb = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(m, dtype=torch.float32))

    def forward(self, x):
        y = x @ self.emb.T
        return torch.cat([x, torch.sin(y), torch.cos(y)], dim=-1)

In practice, the area-weighted blend is applied to the inputs [φ(δ), Z], both feature levels are concatenated, and one shared MLP head runs on the result. This matches the official repository’s layout and keeps the released weights compatible.

5. Full architecture

Image→VGG16-BN conv1–4→conv3 (1/8) · conv4 (1/16)→1×1 conv · ASPP→IFI at every proposal & auxiliary point→shared heads [1024, 512, 256, 256]→ĉ, (Δx, Δy)

THE MODEL WRAPPER

class APGCC(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, cfg):
        super().__init__()
        self.cfg = cfg
        self.encoder = Base_VGG(pretrained=cfg.pretrained_backbone)   # conv1..conv4
        self.decoder = IFI_Decoder(cfg, self.encoder.out_planes)      # ASPP + IFI + heads

    def forward(self, images, targets=None):
        feats = self.encoder(images)
        out, maps, grid_hw = self.decoder(feats)                      # all point proposals
        if self.training and self.cfg.aux_enabled and targets is not None:
            out['aux'] = apg_forward(self.decoder, maps, targets, grid_hw)   # training only
        return out

Auxiliary points exist only during training. At inference APGCC costs the same as the base model: run the network, keep proposals with confidence above 0.5, and the count is how many are left.

6. Losses

The baseline loss is a classification term over all proposals plus a regression term on the matched ones:

ℒcls = −(1/M) ( Σi≤N log ĉψ(i) + λ1 Σi>N log(1 − ĉψ(i)) ) Eq. 2
ℒloc = (1/N) Σi ‖pi − p̂ψ(i)‖²2,    ℒpoint = ℒcls + λ2ℒloc Eq. 3–4

APG adds one term for positives and one for negatives:

ℒposAPG = (1/N kpos) Σ ( −log ĉ*pos + λ3‖p − p̂*pos‖²2 ) Eq. 5
ℒnegAPG = (1/N kneg) Σ ( −log(1 − ĉ*neg) + λ4‖Δ*neg‖²2 ) Eq. 6
ℒoverall = ℒpoint + λ5( ℒposAPG + ℒnegAPG ) Eq. 7, 9

Both APG terms are implemented as cross-entropy losses, as in the official repository.

LOSS COMPUTATION (CONDENSED)

def point_losses(self, out, targets, indices):
    # Eq. (2): CE over all M proposals, unmatched ones are background with weight λ1 = 0.5
    tgt_cls[bidx, sidx] = 1
    l_cls = F.cross_entropy(logits.transpose(1, 2), tgt_cls, self.cls_weight)
    # Eq. (3): squared L2 between matched proposals and their GT, divided by N
    l_loc = F.mse_loss(out['pred_points'][bidx, sidx], tgt, reduction='sum') / n
    return l_cls, l_loc

def apg_loss(self, aux):
    for d in aux['pos']:   # Eq. (5): confidence → 1, prediction → GT
        ce  = F.cross_entropy(d['pred_logits'], ones)
        pos = pos + ce + λ3 * F.mse_loss(d['pred_points'], d['gt'], reduction='sum') / n
    for d in aux['neg']:   # Eq. (6): confidence → 0, offset → 0
        ce  = F.cross_entropy(d['pred_logits'], zeros)
        neg = neg + ce + λ4 * d['offset'].pow(2).sum() / n
    return pos / k_pos, neg / k_neg

# Eq. (4) + (9)
total = l_cls + λ2 * l_loc + λ5 * (pos + neg)        # λ2=λ3=λ4=2e-4, λ5=0.2
SettingValueSettingValue
Stride s · reference points K8 · 4 (8 for QNRF)λ1 (negatives in ℒcls)0.5
Offset scale γ · matching τ100 · 0.05λ2, λ3, λ42 × 10−4

7. Results from the paper

The authors’ reported results across the main benchmarks:

The gains are largest against the method APGCC builds on: compared with P2PNet, MAE falls by about 7% on ShanghaiTech A, 10% on B, 6% on UCF-QNRF, 10% on UCF_CC_50 and 7% on NWPU-Crowd. That's a sizeable improvement for a change that only affects training.
